latin.653: §. 6. Interim quò denegatam à me, Orali Manducationis Corporis Christi, Fundamentalitatem, quòd ad Fidem Christianam attinet, dignè satis ac sensibiliter exprobraret mihi, arguit Clar. Autor §. 14. me negando Articulum de S. Cœna, fundamentalem esse, & mihi ipsi, & Sociis fidei meæ, & Scripturæ S. (quod DEUS prohibeat,) totique Analogiæ fidei contradixisse. Mihi quidem ipsi, dum omnem solumque Articulum in Scriptura S. ad salutem, vel conceptis verbis, vel per evidentem Consequentiam necessarium dictum p. 73. perhibuerim Fundamentalem esse; Atqui in Articulo de Cœna (fortean etiam quoad Oralem Corporis Christi Manducationem) hujusmodi necessitas se prodat manifesta, scil. tam mandati, quando dicitur: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem: quàm medii, siquidem Corpus Christi pro nobis datum.
latin.654: Hic equidem vellem, dum Clarissim. Professor me fingit ipsi mihi contradixisse, ipsemet saltem aliquid dixisse videri posset. Quæ enim qualísque quæso Ratiocinatio hæc: Articulus fundamentalis is omnis & solus est, qui in ipsâ Scriptura S. vel expressis verbis, vel per evidentem Consequentiam, ad salutem absolutè necessarius perhibetur; Articulus autem de S. Cœna necessitatem habet mandati, quia injuncta S. Cœna est; Itemque necessitatem Medii, quia Corpus Christi pro nobis datum est, Ergo Articulus de S. Cœna est fundamentalis. Non omnes hîc tangam scopas parum combinatas; hoc solum quæsivero in præsens ex Autore: Num, quodcunque in Scriptura à Deo mandatum est, eóque necessitatem mandati dicitur habere, idcirco vel conceptis verbis, vel per evidentem Consequentiam, ad salutem absolutè necessarium in Script. S. dictum sit? Vel, quod eôdem redit: num omne Mandatum DEI, absolutè necessarium ad salutem sit? Quodsi hoc; quî ergo isti salvabuntur, qui antequam manducant de pane Sacramentali, de quo mandatum est: Edite hoc est Corpus meum, diem suum obeunt? Num omne Medium salutis, absolutè necessarium ad salutem est? Quomodo igitur Infantes, etiam baptizati, salutem consequentur, si in ætate infantili, auditûs verbi divini, ordinarii Salutis medii, incapaces, ex hac vita discedant?
latin.655: At verò largitus tamen ipsemet sum pag. 80. in Articulo de Cœna: hæresin, latiori scil. sensu, concipi posse; id v. fieri posse num credibile est, quærit A. siquidem iste Articulus ad fundamentum fidei nullatenus pertinet. Resp. Ad fundamentum fidei nullatenus pertinere doctrinam de Regno Millenario Apocalyptico Cap. 20. Obtinueritne jam tum, an verò adhuc exspectandum sit? ipsemet Autor concesserit; intereà quot non numerô hæreses ex exspectato adhuc, eliciunt hodieque Domini Wittebergenses? Atque vel ex hoc ipsô intelliget quoque Vir Clariss. quomodo negando Fundamentalitatem Articuli de Cœna, largiendo interim, hæresin latè sic dictam circa eundem articulum committi posse, FIDEI MEÆ SOCIIS, in specie Neostadiensibus, contradixerim minùs, quin, Articulum de S. Cœna, ad fundamentum fidei haudquaquam referentibus, quædam interim de S. Cœna disputata fundamentum fidei attingere posse hæresímque incurrere fassis, ex asse adstipulatus fuerim, præsertim cùm iisdem propemodum verbis, (quibus illi Certamina de S. Cœna, non meras logomachias deque lana caprina contentiones esse perhibent,) idem asseruerim. Quando verò tertió locô, SCRIPTURÆ quoque S. me contradicere ex eo annititur probare, quòd Scriptura ten didachen baptísmon, vel, doctrinam de Baptismate, ad themelion, seu fundamentum referat. Hebr. 6, 2. S. Cœna v. perinde atque Baptismus Sacramentum sit; næ ille multò evidentiùs quàm volet, propria vineta cædit, S. Cœnam quidem perinde atque Baptismum, pro Sacramentis habentia, Necessitatem verò horum ad salutem multis gradibus discriminatam, agnoscentia, ita scil. ut Baptismi necessitatem absolutam statuant, indeque de non baptizatorum, utut Christianorum, Infantum salute, ægrè persuadeantur, saltem de eadem plurimùm hæsitent, S. Cœnæ etiam necessitatem, non nisi ordinatam admittant, cujus non privatio, sed solus contemptus, damnat. Quartò, dum A. contradictionem à me, ut ipsi videtur, adversus totam fidei Analogiam, designatam, ad eam Contradictionem postliminio coërcet, quæ cum solâ S. Cœnæ Natura & Indole, pugnat, nova nullâ hujus Contradictionis probatione adjectâ, præter eas, quibus in Anti-Irenico suo Tractatu, pro Fundamentalitate Articuli de S. Cœna decertaverat, vadimonium deficit & magno promisso cadit hiatu.
latin.656: §. VII. Verùm enim verò probationum harum, ad quinarium numerum redactarum vindicatio, postremum eorum omnium est, quô in aciem disputatoriam adversus me, pacem unionémque cum ejus Ecclesiâ Christianè ambientem, prodire ipsi volupe fuit, cujus imbecillitatem postquam ostenderimus, Annotationi nostræ de Manducatione Corporis Christi Orali, Disputationíque contra istius partim Veritatem, partim, si Veritas supponatur, Fundamentalitatem, seu ad salutem vel creditu, vel factu, Necessitatem, finem imponemus. Sicuti verò prima Clarissimi Professoris Probatio, Articulum de S. Cœna fundamentalem esse, vel rectiùs, Oralem Corporis Christi in S. Cœna Manducationem, salvâ, (ut habent verba Autoris) hominis fide, lædi à quoquam temerè, aut infirmari, nedum negari, posse, in eo robur suum collocatum habet, quòd Oralis Manducatio inter bona à Servatore nostro, testamento nobis legata, annumeranda supponit, ita, ut, cùm advertisset Autor, tantopere à se commendatam Oralem Manducationem, Testamentariis Salvatoris nostri bonis propriè dictis, à me neutiquam accenseri, ceu ad solos Christi discipulos, veros unicosque hæredes ejus & cohæredes, pertinentibus, contendit, Bona Testamentaria quæ merentur dici, non ex conditione hæredum, sed ex ipsâ rerum natura & voluntate Testatoris, esse judicandum: Distinguendum item esse inter Bona Testamentaria & inter Commoda ex bonis istis redundantia, §. XV.
latin.657: Resp. Ne ad logomachias cum Autore deveniendum sit, ponamus (1) Testamentariorum bonorum nomine, omnia in universum N. Fœderis Bona, eóque etiam ea, quæ improbis juxta ac Fidelibus sunt communia, venire; licèt interim certum sit, (a) Testamentaria bona N. Test. in Sacrâ Script. illa propriè dici, quæ hæredibus Christi cedunt, hæredes autem, Christi solos DEI filios constitui: Unde Apostolus: Quodsi Filii, etiam hæredes, nempe DEI hæredes & cohæredes Christi Rom. 8, 17. Gal. 4, 7. (b) Certum sit, Spiritualem Manducationem Corporis Christi, i.e. intimam cum Christo communionem hæredibus Christi propriam manere. (c) Certum sit juxta ipsum Lutherum, tam promissionem Christi omnem, quas inter & promissio de Corpore Christi manducando locum reperit, citra fidem, obtineri non posse cum sine Controversia promissio & fides correlativa sint, & ubi fides non fuerit, promissio nihil sit, Tom. 2. Jen. fol. 452. b. in f. quam hæredes solos eos esse, qui credunt Testamento, ibid. f. 455. a. in f.
latin.658: (2) Ponamus, inter Bona Testamentaria, & Commoda inde oriunda, discriminandum, cùm alias Bona, & Commoda, probe inter se conspirent, Bonaque etiam Commodorum nomine, & vice versâ Commoda nomine Bonorum, appellari queant, tamen istud extra dubium mecum posuerit Autor, Testamentaria bona, si de iis indiscriminatim omnibus sermo sit, non esse ejusdem rationis & ponderis, eorumque alia necessariam, alia minùs necessariam cum salute æterna habere connexionem; hôcque extra dubium positô, vel ipsum arbitrum appello Disputatorem: Num Oralis Manducatio corporis Christi, etiamsi vera foret, per se solam considerata, prioris, an verò posterioris potiùs generis bonis Testamentariis annumeranda veniat? Quodsi a. ad posterioris generis Bona Testamentaria, Oralis Manducatio, si vera sit, pertinet, (quemadmodum ex dictâ hypothesi, ad hæc omnino, non autem priora, pertinere ex eo manifestum evadit, quòd; ex aliâ Autoris hypothesi, multi Oraliter Corpus Christi manducent, qui æternum tamen pereant) utique constat, Doctrinam de Orali Manducatione non esse fidei Christianæ fundamentalem & per consequens, dissensum in hac Doctrina, non esse dissensum Fidei fundamentalem, tantóque minùs; quanto inter ita dissidentes, magis convenit, Spiritualem Manducationem corporis Christi, etiam citra omnem Sacramentalem, ad salutem æternam obtinendam sufficere, quin, dum intimam hæc cum Christo Unionem Communionémque absolvit, vitæ eam æternæ, Spiritualiter Corpus Christi manducantibus testamento à Christo legatæ, primitias præbere: Quorsum pertinet istud, paulò post Institutionem S. Cœnæ, discipulis suis, spirituali Manducatione usis, à Christo dictum: Kagō diatithemai hymin basileian &c. Et ego vobis Testamento addico Regnum, ut edatis & bibatis ad mensam meam in Regno meo, Luc. 22, 29. & 30.

pass_a.653: §. 6. Meanwhile, that he might reproach me worthily enough and sensibly for the Fundamentalitatem of the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body denied by me as concerns the Christian Faith, the Famous Author argues in §. 14 that by denying the Article on the Sacred Supper to be fundamental I have contradicted myself, and my faith’s Companions, and Sacred Scripture (which GOD forbid), and the whole Analogy of faith. Myself indeed, while at p. 73 I had held every and only Article in Sacred Scripture said necessary to salvation — either in express words or by evident Consequence — to be Fundamental; And yet in the Article on the Supper (perhaps even as to the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body) this kind of necessity shows itself manifest — namely both of mandate, when it is said: Do this in remembrance of me; and of means, seeing Christ’s Body was given for us.
pass_a.654: Here indeed I would wish, while the most Famous Professor feigns that I have contradicted myself, that he himself might at least seem to have said something. For what and of what sort, I ask, is this Reasoning: That fundamental Article is every and only one which in Sacred Scripture itself is held absolutely necessary to salvation either in express words or by evident Consequence; But the Article on the Sacred Supper has necessity of mandate, because the Sacred Supper is enjoined; And likewise necessity of Means, because Christ’s Body was given for us; Therefore the Article on the Sacred Supper is fundamental. I will not touch here all the poorly combined targets; this alone I will ask for the present from the Author: Whether whatever is commanded by God in Scripture, and so is said to have necessity of mandate, is therefore said in Sacred Scripture — either in express words or by evident Consequence — to be absolutely necessary to salvation? Or, what comes to the same: whether every Command of GOD is absolutely necessary to salvation? If so, how then will those be saved who before they eat of the Sacramental bread, of which the command is: Eat, this is my Body, meet their day? Is every Medium of salvation absolutely necessary to salvation? How then will Infants, even baptized, obtain salvation, if in infant age, incapable of the hearing of the divine word — the ordinary Medium of Salvation — they depart this life?
pass_a.655: But yet I myself granted at p. 80 in the Article on the Supper that heresy can be conceived in a wider sense; and whether that can happen is credible, asks A., if this Article in no way pertains to the foundation of faith. Resp. That the doctrine of the Millennial Kingdom of Apocalypse ch. 20 in no way pertains to the foundation of faith — whether it already obtained then, or is still to be awaited — the Author himself will have conceded; meanwhile how many heresies do the Wittenberg Lords even today elicit from what is still awaited? And from this very thing the most Famous Man will also understand how, by denying the Fundamentalitatem of the Article on the Supper while granting meantime that heresy broadly so called can be committed about the same article, I have contradicted my FAITH’S COMPANIONS — specially the Neostadians — the less, nay rather have wholly agreed with those who, not referring the Article on the Sacred Supper to the foundation of faith at all, yet confessed that certain things disputed about the Sacred Supper can touch the foundation of faith and incur heresy — especially since in nearly the same words (by which they hold the Contests on the Sacred Supper not to be mere word-fights and contentions about goat’s wool) I asserted the same. But when in the third place he strives to prove that I also contradict SACRED SCRIPTURE from this — that Scripture refers the teaching of baptisms, or the doctrine of Baptism, to the foundation (Heb. 6:2), and the Sacred Supper likewise with Baptism is a Sacrament — nay he cuts his own vineyards much more evidently than he will wish: those who hold the Sacred Supper likewise with Baptism for Sacraments, yet acknowledge their Necessity to salvation discriminated by many grades — so namely that they establish Baptism’s necessity as absolute, and thence are hardly persuaded of the salvation of unbaptized Infants even of Christians, or at least hesitate much about the same, while they admit even the Sacred Supper’s necessity only as ordained, whose deprivation does not damn, but only contempt. Fourth, while A. forces the contradiction designated by me, as it seems to him, against the whole Analogy of faith back at last to that Contradiction which fights with the Sacred Supper’s Nature and Character alone, with no new proof of this Contradiction added beyond those by which in his Anti-Irenic Tract he had fought for the Fundamentalitatem of the Article on the Sacred Supper, he forfeits his bail and falls with a great promised gap.
pass_a.656: §. VII. But indeed the vindication of these proofs, reduced to the number five, is the last of all those things by which it was pleasant to him to come forth into disputatory battle against me, Christianly seeking peace and union with his Church — whose weakness after we have shown, we will set an end to our Annotation on the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body, and to the Disputation against its Truth in part, and in part, if Truth be supposed, against its Fundamentalitatem, or Necessity to salvation either for believing or for doing. But as the most Famous Professor’s first Proof — that the Article on the Sacred Supper is fundamental, or more rightly, that the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body in the Sacred Supper cannot, faith being safe (as the Author’s words have it), be rashly wounded by anyone, or weakened, much less denied — has its strength placed in this, that it supposes Oral Eating to be numbered among the goods bequeathed to us by our Savior in the testament, so that, when the Author had noticed that the Oral Eating so greatly commended by him is in no way counted by me among our Savior’s Testamentary goods properly so called, as pertaining to Christ’s disciples alone, His true and only heirs and co-heirs, he contends that Testamentary Goods which deserve to be so called are to be judged not from the heirs’ condition but from the things’ own nature and the Testator’s will: And that distinction is also to be made between Testamentary Goods and the Commodities overflowing from those goods, §. XV.
pass_a.657: Resp. Lest we come to word-fights with the Author, let us posit (1) that under the name of Testamentary goods there come all the New Covenant’s Goods in general, and so also those which are common to the wicked equally with the Faithful; although meantime it is certain (a) that those Testamentary goods of the New Testament are properly so called in Sacred Scripture which fall to Christ’s heirs, and that Christ’s heirs are constituted only the sons of GOD: Whence the Apostle: And if sons, then also heirs — namely GOD’s heirs and Christ’s co-heirs, Rom. 8:17, Gal. 4:7. (b) It is certain that the Spiritual Eating of Christ’s Body — i.e. intimate communion with Christ — remains proper to Christ’s heirs. (c) It is certain according to Luther himself that every promise of Christ — among which the promise concerning eating Christ’s Body also finds place — cannot be obtained apart from faith, since without Controversy promise and faith are correlative, and where faith has not been, the promise is nothing (Tom. 2 Jena fol. 452 b. at end), and that only those are heirs who believe the Testament (ibid. fol. 455 a. at end).
pass_a.658: (2) Let us posit that discrimination is to be made between Testamentary Goods and the Commodities arising thence — although otherwise Goods and Commodities well conspire with each other, and Goods can also be called by the name of Commodities and conversely Commodities by the name of Goods — yet the Author will have placed this with me beyond doubt: that Testamentary goods, if speech is of them all indiscriminately, are not of the same reason and weight, and that some of them have a necessary, others a less necessary, connection with eternal salvation; and this being placed beyond doubt, I even call the Disputator himself as arbiter: Whether the Oral Eating of Christ’s body, even if it were true, considered by itself alone, is to be numbered among Testamentary goods of the prior, or rather of the posterior, kind? But if Oral Eating, if it be true, pertains to Testamentary Goods of the posterior kind (as from the said hypothesis it becomes clear that it pertains altogether to these, not to the prior — because from the Author’s other hypothesis many eat Christ’s Body Oraliter who yet perish eternally), it certainly stands that the Doctrine of Oral Eating is not fundamental to the Christian faith, and consequently dissent in this Doctrine is not a fundamental dissent of Faith — and so much the less, the more it is agreed among those so dissenting that the Spiritual Eating of Christ’s body, even apart from all Sacramental, suffices to obtaining eternal salvation — nay, while it completes intimate Union and Communion with Christ, it affords the firstfruits of that eternal life bequeathed by testament from Christ to those spiritually eating Christ’s Body: Whither pertains that said by Christ a little after the Institution of the Sacred Supper to His disciples who had used spiritual Eating: And I assign to you by Testament a Kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom, Luke 22:29–30.

653: §.IV §.6: Author §.14 reproaches Strimesius for denying Oral’s Fundamentalitatem — claiming contradiction of self, faith-companions, Scripture, and the analogy of faith.
The charge turns on Strimesius’s own rule (p. 73): only Scripture-necessary articles are fundamental — and the Author says the Supper shows mandate (‘do this’) and means (body given for us).
654: The Author’s syllogism — mandate + means ⇒ fundamental Supper article — does not hold. Not every divine command is absolutely necessary to salvation (else who dies before eating the sacramental bread?).
Not every salvation-medium is absolute either — baptized infants die without hearing the word, the ordinary medium.
655: Strimesius already granted (p. 80) heresy in a wide sense about the Supper. The millennium (Rev. 20) also fails the faith-foundation test, yet Wittenberg still wrings heresies from it. Denying Supper-fundamentality while allowing broad heresy matches his Neostadian companions.

Heb. 6:2 on baptism-as-foundation cuts the Author’s own vineyard: baptism’s necessity is treated as absolute, the Supper’s only as ordained (contempt damns, not mere deprivation). The analogy-of-faith charge collapses back into the Anti-Irenicum’s old proofs — bail forfeited.
656: §.VII: last of five proofs — then this Oral Annotation ends. The first proof’s strength is counting Oral among testamentary goods bequeathed by the Savior.

Because Strimesius will not count Oral among testamentary goods proper to Christ’s true heirs alone, the Author (§.XV) says judge such goods by the testator’s will/nature of the things, and distinguish goods from overflowing commodities.
657: Reply (1): grant ‘testamentary goods’ can name all New-Covenant goods, even those common to wicked and faithful — yet Scripture properly calls testamentary those that fall to Christ’s heirs, and heirs are only God’s sons (Rom. 8:17; Gal. 4:7).

Spiritual eating (intimate communion) remains proper to those heirs. Luther: every promise — including eating Christ’s body — is nothing without correlative faith; only testament-believers are heirs (Jena Tom. 2).
658: §.IV close: even granting a goods/commodities split, and that testamentary goods differ in weight toward eternal salvation — Oral, if true, belongs to the lesser class (many oral eaters still perish).

So Oral doctrine is not faith-fundamental; dissent here is not fundamental dissent — the more so as spiritual eating apart from sacramental suffices for eternal life and already gives its firstfruits (Luke 22:29–30: kingdom by testament to eat and drink at His table). Stop before Annotatio V §.V.
